name: Jade Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on an overhead crew out of the east depot, four of us and a bucket truck. We start at seven with a tailboard talk, which is the safety chat at the back of the truck, then it's whatever the day throws at us: swapping a rotten pole, changing out a transformer, re-sagging a line a lorry clipped. I love the bit up in the bucket when the job's going right and nobody's talking. What wears me out is storm season, sixteen-hour shifts and then the paperwork on that new tablet they gave us.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Theo in a rented flat above a bakery on Mill Road, so I wake up smelling bread at four. Theo drives the number 12 bus for the city. We've got about three months of money put by, which feels okay until the landlord sends one of his letters. I'm in the union, I go to most branch meetings, and I'm the one who still writes her hours in a paper notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Everyone at the depot was waiting for the robots and the clever software, and it turned out to be a fancier spellcheck. I'd post something like, the poles are still wood and the wires are still live, so call a lineworker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my job's fine. Nobody's building a machine that can climb a cracked pole in the rain on Fenwick Lane at two in the morning. The only thing that changes is the office gets a few more shortcuts, and that's their business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd keep putting a bit from every overtime check into savings, aiming for six months instead of three. And I'd keep pushing at branch meetings for a proper storm-pay deal, because that's the fight that actually matters to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest. It's the world I already know how to live in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the tablet. What does it do now, and would that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's where the work orders come in, and it wants photos and boxes ticked for everything. If AI fills in a few of those boxes for me, fine, I won't complain, but I won't go looking for it either. I'll keep my paper notebook as a backup because the tablet dies in the cold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that worries you even if AI stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent, mainly. Our landlord put it up last spring and he's hinting again. With three months saved we're not in trouble, but we're never going to buy a place on Mill Road at this rate. That's not an AI problem, that's just how it is for people our age.

say: The **poles are still wood** and the wires are still live, so call a lineworker.
AI turned out to be a **fancier spellcheck**, not the end of skilled trades.
think: My **job is safe**, because nobody builds a machine to climb a cracked pole at night.
Only the **office** gets shortcuts, and that's not my concern.
do: Keep working the **overhead crew** as normal and keep the paper notebook as a backup.
Build savings from **three to six months** using overtime money.
Push at **branch meetings** for a better storm-pay deal.
feel: **Relieved** and a little smug that her world stays the same.
S0.quote: Nobody's building a machine that can climb a cracked pole in the rain on Fenwick Lane at two in the morning.
fieldNote: Her sense of **security** rests on the physical danger and mess of the work.
**Rent** is her real background worry, and she separates it clearly from AI.
She'd accept small tablet help but **won't seek** AI out.

steps.text: Keep climbing with the east depot crew as usual
Move overtime money into savings until six months are covered
Raise storm pay at every union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office getting hit, not us. I'd tell the lads at the depot to be nice to the planners, because they're the ones whose jobs are going into a computer. Online I'd say the union needs to get ahead of this now, not after the redundancy letters go out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it squeezes us in sneaky ways. If software plans the routes and hands out the jobs, it'll plan us tighter, with less slack and less overtime. My pay leans on overtime more than I'd like to admit, maybe a fifth of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union rep straight away and ask what's in the next contract about software scheduling. I'd keep a record of my own hours on paper, so if the system shaves time off I can prove it. And I'd stop counting on overtime for the savings and put a fixed amount aside every month instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not the end of the world for me, but I hate the idea of a program deciding how hard I work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would feel this first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marguerite in planning, for sure. She's been doing switching schedules for twenty years and she's the person who knows which feeder is dodgy. If they swap her for software, we lose that knowledge and somebody gets hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Theo and the bus?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Theo's fine for a while, I think. Buses are hands-on, and the card says robots come slowly. But he's already seeing ticket machines and an app that tells him off for braking hard, so he's grumpy about it.

say: The **planners** get hit first, so be kind to the office staff.
The union needs to act **before redundancy letters** go out, not after.
think: Software scheduling will plan crews **tighter**, with less slack and less overtime.
About **a fifth** of her pay comes from overtime, and that's exposed.
do: Ask the **union rep** what the next contract says about software scheduling.
Log her own hours **on paper** to catch any time shaved off.
Save a **fixed monthly amount** instead of relying on overtime.
feel: **Uneasy**, and angry at the idea of a program setting her workload.
S1.quote: If software plans the routes and hands out the jobs, it'll plan us tighter, with less slack and less overtime.
fieldNote: She sees the threat as **control over work**, not losing the job outright.
Her worry for Marguerite is about **safety knowledge** walking out the door.
**Overtime dependence** is a gap she hasn't fully faced before.

steps.text: Ask the union rep about software scheduling in the next contract
Keep a paper log of every shift and callout
Set aside a fixed sum each month instead of overtime money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union and a government with a spine. Out loud I'd be calling for the power company to stay public and for any robot crews to be run by people, not a tech firm. I'd be at every march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? I think I'm out of a job by about 2031, and so is Theo. A robot that climbs as well as me and doesn't need a tailboard talk, why would the company keep me? I'd be thirty-one with no plan B, because I never wanted one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd get the whole branch pushing for a no-redundancy deal and retraining money. I'd stop any big spending, no holiday, no new car, and get our savings as high as they'll go. I'd probably vote for whoever promises to tax the robot owners, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, if I'm honest. Picturing it makes my stomach drop, the way it does when you hear a line hum that shouldn't be live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So the thinking side changes in 2028 and the climbing side around 2031. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gap is three years of watching it come. The office goes first, and then they send a robot out with us to learn, and we're basically training our own replacement. I'd hate every day of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Theo say to each other that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd say something stupid like at least we'll both be home for dinner. Then we'd do the sums on the back of an envelope and realise three months of savings doesn't stretch across two lost jobs. I think we'd sit there quiet for a long time.

say: Keep the **power company public** and robot crews run by people.
She'd be at **every march** and every branch meeting.
think: She expects both she and Theo to **lose their jobs** by about 2031.
At thirty-one she'd have **no plan B**, because she never wanted one.
do: Push the branch for a **no-redundancy deal** and retraining money in year one.
Cancel the **holiday and car** and grow savings as far as possible.
Vote for whoever promises to **tax robot owners**.
feel: **Sick** and frightened, like hearing a line hum that shouldn't be live.
S2.quote: A robot that climbs as well as me and doesn't need a tailboard talk, why would the company keep me?
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** reads to her as training her own replacement.
Two **household earners** exposed at once is what tips her into alarm.
Her resistance shows as having **no fallback** rather than denial.

steps.text: Organise the branch to demand a no-redundancy deal
Cancel the summer holiday and the car loan plans
Vote and campaign for a tax on robot owners

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, louder, and with more time to make it stick. I'd say we've got a few years, so let's write the rules now: robots on the lines need a human crew lead, and the savings go to the workers. I'd say it in the canteen and I'd say it to our local councillor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives the union time to win something, and that's the only hope I've got. My job probably still goes in the end, around 2034, when I'd be thirty-five. But maybe as the person who watches the robot instead of the person it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the branch's working group on new technology, even though I'd rather eat the tablet. I'd save hard for five years, because that's enough time to get to a proper cushion. And Theo and I would hold off on trying to buy a flat until we know what's left standing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. Five years is like a storm forecast: you hate it, but you can stack the trucks and get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never want a plan B. Does five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it does, a bit. I'd still not go chasing computer courses, but I might do the cable jointing certificate, because underground work in tight holes feels like the last thing a robot gets good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have about five years before AGI and eight before the robots. How would you use that time with the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray, my old foreman who retired last year, always said the crews that complain loudest get the best contracts. I'd make sure we were loud. Five years is long enough to be a nuisance.

say: Use the time to **write the rules**: a human crew lead with every robot.
Tell the canteen and the **local councillor** the savings belong to workers.
think: Her job probably still **goes around 2034**, when she's thirty-five.
The only hope is the union winning a **watcher role** instead of replacement.
do: Join the branch **technology working group** despite hating the tablet.
Save hard for **five years** to build a proper cushion.
Hold off on **buying a flat** with Theo until things settle.
feel: **Anxious** but able to prepare, like getting ready for a storm forecast.
S3.quote: Five years is like a storm forecast: you hate it, but you can stack the trucks and get ready.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her alarm into **organising energy**.
She'd consider **cable jointing**, a hands-on retrain she sees as robot-proof.
She still refuses **computer courses**, true to her resistance.

steps.text: Join the union branch's working group on new technology
Take the underground cable jointing certificate
Postpone buying a flat with Theo for now
Save a fixed sum monthly for five years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for the bosses to plan our exit, so we'd better plan our side. Publicly I'd keep the same line: public power, people in charge of the machines. I'd probably be on the branch committee by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it scares me less, but it doesn't go away. In 2039 I'd be forty. Forty is old to start again but young to retire, so I'd be stuck in the middle with a trade that doesn't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on climbing, but I'd do the cable jointing ticket in the first couple of years and maybe a substation course after. I'd keep saving the fixed amount. And I'd stand for the branch committee so I'm in the room when they negotiate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a slow, background way. Like a tooth that aches when you drink something cold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, where do you picture yourself in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the apprentice to learn the hands-on stuff properly but not to bet their whole life on it. Ten years is a career for them, and it'd end right when they get good. I'd feel awful saying it, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new apprentice starting at the depot under this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Terrible. I'd also tell them to join the union on their first day, because forty-year-olds like me will need all the votes we can get.

say: Ten years means the bosses **plan our exit**, so workers must plan too.
She'd stand for the **branch committee** to be in the room.
think: In 2039 she'd be **forty**, too old to start again and too young to retire.
The fear is **smaller but constant**, not gone.
do: Keep climbing while taking the **cable jointing ticket** early.
Add a **substation course** later in the decade.
Keep saving a **fixed amount** every month.
feel: A slow, background **ache** of worry that never fully goes.
S4.quote: In 2039 I'd be forty. Forty is old to start again but young to retire, so I'd be stuck in the middle with a trade that doesn't exist.
fieldNote: More time softens the fear but **does not change** where she ends up.
Her advice to apprentices shows **guilt** about the trade's future.
She relies on **collective power** over personal reinvention.

steps.text: Stand for the union branch committee within two years
Take cable jointing first, then a substation course
Keep saving the same fixed sum each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because it takes Theo and me out at the same time and we've only got three months saved. What would help is a law that says if a company swaps people for robots, the workers get paid while they retrain, and the union gets a seat at the table. Not a leaflet, actual money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but if a robot drops a live conductor on my crew, who's responsible? I want to know that before anyone puts one up a pole.

headlineQuote: If a robot drops a live conductor on my crew, who's responsible? I want to know that before anyone puts one up a pole.
portrait: Jade is a 27-year-old **overhead lineworker** at a city depot who loves the quiet of the bucket.
She rents on Mill Road with **Theo**, a bus driver, with about three months saved.
A committed **union member**, she blames bosses and wants power kept public.
She calls the slow scenarios safe but sees AGI by 2028 as **losing both jobs**.
She refuses AI tools and pins her hopes on **collective action** and hands-on retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Theo could lose their jobs together on a thin cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A law giving workers **paid retraining** and the union a seat when robots replace people.
